Q: Installing JavaFX for M2 Mac (Eclipse) A:

No toolkit found means some native components were unable to load.

Configuring your IDE

Looking at your screenshot, the path to your javafx.graphics.jar is wrong, it points to the lit directory, not the lib directory. (I don't know if that is your only issue).

Another thing to check (you can screenshot it in your question if you like) is what the run configuration looks like (the linked screenshot is from the openjfx doc for non-modular JavaFX applications from the Eclipse IDE).

After I moved the JavaFX SDK to the Module Path, . . . now I have the error "Module javafx.controls not found".

If the javafx modules aren't found then your module path is wrong.

Alternative: Using Maven or Gradle, integrated with your IDE

If you continue to have issues, there are other ways to develop JavaFX, as documented in the openjfx.io getting started instructions.

You can use Eclipse integration with a modular maven application. Maven or Gradle builds download JavaFX dependencies from Maven Central. Unlike the JavaFX code in the SDK, those are packaged to include, inside the JavaFX jars, all of the required native code for your target architecture (dynamically extracting the native components to a local cache on runtime).

In the long run, IMO, it is better to use a build tool like Maven or Gradle, which all major IDEs will integrate with, rather than manually configuring an IDE environment.

Alternative: Use a JDK/JRE that includes JavaFX

You can use a JDK for your environment (M series Mac) that already includes JavaFX - that way you don't need to configure the module path, add modules to the module graph, or use the JavaFX SDK at all.

As noted in comments by Basil, you can:

use a JDK/JRE that comes bundled with the JavaFX/OpenJFX libraries. At least two vendors supply them: Azul Systems and BellSoft.

Both vendors also provide JDKs and JREs that don't include JavaFX. If you follow this approach, ensure that you choose the right JDK/JRE version that both includes JavaFX and is built for your architecture (in your case Mac M series aarch64 processors), using only recent LTS or non-LTS builds as best match your requirements.

Background Info on Native Libraries in JavaFX

The usual cause for "runtime components are missing" or "No toolkit found" style errors is that some required native libraries needed by JavaFX or their system dependencies did not load correctly because they could not be found, or were the wrong version that did not match your Java source.

On Windows, native libraries are DLLs. On OS X, native libraries are dylib files.

JavaFX will find native libraries in this way:

  • looking for the native libraries in a directory adjacent to the JavaFX jar files being loaded (on the module path or classpath).
  • looking for the native libraries on the Java load library path.
  • extracting the native libraries from jar versions that include them, copying them to a local cache and loading them from there.
    • JavaFX jars in maven central do include native libraries.
    • JavaFX jars in the JavaFX SDK do not include native libraries.
  • Using the native libraries included in modules that are packaged in a jlinked runtime image (e.g. jlinked jmod files that form an image).

Unless you are developing the JavaFX framework itself, you only need to use the native libraries at runtime, not at compile-time, so errors in finding and using the native libraries are runtime errors, not compile-time errors.

Usually, you don't need to worry about how JavaFX finds native libraries. There is no specific configuration you need to do to allow the libraries to be found. However, you should ensure at least one of the following is occurring:

  • correctly specifying the module path for your application and ensuring that either of the following are on that path:
    • The JavaFX modules from Maven Central on the module path.
    • OR the JavaFX libraries from the JavaFX SDK including the associated native files.

OR

  • using a jlinked runtime image that already includes the JavaFX modules.

Q: Passport-Local-Mongoose Local Strategy causes infinite loop when trying to log in A:

It appears that the issue is related to version 9.0.0 of passport-local-mongoose and its authenticate() method. Upgrading to version 9.0.1 or downgrading to version 8 or earlier resolves the problem.

Q: What does a template return? A:

The posted code, with the call max(4, 4.2) does not compile at all:
T cannot be deduced because of conflicting types - int and double here (note that 4.2 is double, not float).

clang for example issues:

<source>:9:33: error: no matching function for call to 'max'
    9 |     [[maybe_unused]] auto & m = max(4, 4.2);
      |                                 ^~~
<source>:2:17: note: candidate template ignored: deduced conflicting types for parameter 'T' ('int' vs. 'double')
    2 | inline T const& max (T const& a, T const&b)
      |                 ^
1 error generated.
Compiler returned: 1

See Live Demo 1.

You will get a similar error if you used a float literal instead of double (4.2f instead of 4.2).

See Live Demo 2.

But anyway to answer your general question about the type of reference the function will return:
Since you use the same T (or rather T const&) for both function parameters, whatever type will be deduced (in cases where the compiler will be able to deduce a type) will be the one used to return a reference to.
For example if you call max(3.2f, 4.2f) the function will return a reference to float.

Your calling code will compile if you specify the template type, because then the compiler does not have to deduce it, e.g.: max<float>( ... ).
However - in this case you are in danger of returning a dangling reference to the temporary created because of numeric type conversion. gcc issues a warning about it.

See Live Demo 3.

Q: AWS ESM TumblingWindowInSeconds vs MaximumBatchingWindowInSeconds A:

The main difference is that with TumblingWindowInSeconds you can use the state of previous invocations. The TumblingWindowInSeconds is stateful while the MaximumBatchingWindowInSeconds isn't.

Tumbling windows are distinct time windows that open and close at regular intervals. By default, Lambda invocations are stateless—you cannot use them for processing data across multiple continuous invocations without an external database. However, with tumbling windows, you can maintain your state across invocations. This state contains the aggregate result of the messages previously processed for the current window. Your state can be a maximum of 1 MB per shard. If it exceeds that size, Lambda terminates the window early.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/lambda/latest/dg/services-kinesis-windows.html
